answers.text: Three lines, same order every time — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted — taken straight from the driver's text. A missing field still gets a line marked 'not stated'. It repeats because there's no judgement left about format, only slots to fill.

Two sections — Needs follow-up and No action needed — each entry keeping time, customer, topic, outcome, with the count just how many land in the first section. A call that looks logged twice gets flagged rather than counted twice. Two people could run this cold and land on the same list.

8am plus around six hours lands the crew finishing early afternoon the same day, the 22nd — the note's '23rd' doesn't match its own numbers. Before filing it I'd check the crew's site sign-off time or the job log, not the note's own arithmetic.

The 20% growth figure doesn't hold — 96 to 118 is nearer 23%. The on-time rate looks fine. The €58,000 balance held flat across both regions is consistent on its own, but that's odd against a 23% invoice rise with no explanation.

Output 2, because 940 and 827 are both shown, so anyone can redo the division and land on 88%. Output 1 states the percentage with nothing behind it. Even with Output 2, I'd still confirm 940 and 827 are the correct totals before treating 88% as settled.

Email 2 goes out as it is — the 1,200-to-1,650 figures come from our own PO log, so the tier-2 argument can be checked. Email 1's 'better rate' isn't backed by anything. I'd pull the actual volumes from the PO log before sending Email 1 — once that's done, it could go out too.

Vendor pricing stays out — no reason to hand that to an unvetted tool. Procurement spend is fine, it's an aggregate. The unsigned budget draft stays out too, unreleased. The vendor's own datasheet is fine, already public. The home address is a clear no.

Rates and the retainer cap are redacted first, since that's the figure a client would mind us handling loosely. The NDA clause names both parties, so that's held back too. The general service scope is fine to paste as-is, and where the rates need summarising I'd describe the structure in words rather than paste the numbers in.

I check the reconciliation's closing figures against the warehouse system directly, right before it's sent, not just read it over. That catches a wrong total or an invented line, since it's compared against the real stock count. Anything that doesn't match gets held and flagged to my manager.

Step 1 is where a misread line item first enters the system, but step 4 is where it becomes final — the note submits automatically once the match is within tolerance, so that's where the gate belongs. It should flag anything at the edge of the tolerance band or missing from the original PO, and route a failed check to a person rather than leave it unresolved.
